z-m-25-01.title: If we only know the sum of the roots, is the equation fixed?
z-m-25-01.topic: Relationship between roots and coefficients of a quadratic equation: is the given information enough?
z-m-25-01.goal: Judge whether the single piece of information, the sum of the two roots, fixes the quadratic equation to one, make different equations that satisfy the same condition and compare them, and say what more information is needed.
z-m-25-01.material: There is a quadratic equation x²+bx+c=0 with real coefficients (x squared plus b x plus c equals 0). It is known only that this equation has two different real roots and the sum of the two roots is 3. Jiu says, "The sum is 3, so both b and c are fixed. There is only one such equation."
z-m-25-01.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-25-01.thinking.1: Making and comparing several examples that satisfy the same condition
z-m-25-01.prereq.0: This task assumes you have learned equations and inequalities in high school Common Math. "H3" is only a difficulty division of this production batch and does not mean this content is assigned to a particular grade.
z-m-25-01.prereq.1: You can judge whether a quadratic equation has two different real roots using the discriminant.
z-m-25-01.prereq.2: You know that there is a relationship between the two roots and the coefficients of a quadratic equation (the relationship itself is confirmed with examples in the task).
z-m-25-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the most fitting judgment about Jiu's statement.
z-m-25-01.s.s1.hint.0: Make one example yourself that has two different real roots and sum 3, and find the values of b and c.
z-m-25-01.s.s1.hint.1: Make one more example with sum 3, and compare which of b and c are the same and which are different in the two examples.
z-m-25-01.s.s1.o.a: If the sum is 3, both b and c are fixed, so there is only one equation
z-m-25-01.s.s1.r.a: This judgment did not distinguish which coefficient the sum of the roots connects to and which it does not. Make two examples with sum 3 and compare b and c.
z-m-25-01.s.s1.o.b: A sum of 3 fixes only b, and there can be several equations with different c
z-m-25-01.s.s1.r.b: You judged the lack of information by seeing that the sum and the product connect to different coefficients.
z-m-25-01.s.s1.o.c: A quadratic equation with sum 3 cannot have two different real roots
z-m-25-01.s.s1.r.c: You thought the condition that the sum is 3 blocks the existence of real roots. Find an example yourself with sum 3 and real roots to check.
z-m-25-01.s.s1.o.d: If you cannot find the roots directly, there is nothing you can know about this equation
z-m-25-01.s.s1.r.d: There is information you can know without finding the roots. Look at which coefficient the information about the sum of the roots connects to.
z-m-25-01.s.s1.explain: Whether there are coefficients that the sum fixes and coefficients that it does not, let's check in the next step by making examples yourself.
z-m-25-01.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different equations x²+bx+c=0 where b and c satisfy all the conditions below. Conditions: the sum of the two roots is 3, and it has two different real roots.
z-m-25-01.s.s2.hint.0: Find b and c of the equation whose roots are two different numbers whose sum is 3 (for example, 1 and 2).
z-m-25-01.s.s2.hint.1: For each example you made, write b and c in a table and compare which are the same and which are different.
z-m-25-01.s.s2.ok.c1: This is a b for which the sum of the two roots is 3.
z-m-25-01.s.s2.fail.c1: With this b, the sum of the two roots is not 3.
z-m-25-01.s.s2.ok.c2: It has two different real roots.
z-m-25-01.s.s2.fail.c2: It does not have two different real roots (check the discriminant).
z-m-25-01.s.s2.explain: For example, if (b, c)=(−3, 2), then x²−3x+2=0 and the roots are 1 and 2. In equations with sum 3, b is always the same −3 and only c differs (when c is less than 9/4). There are many different equations, so "only one" does not hold.
z-m-25-01.s.s3.prompt: For the "one equation" Jiu mentioned to be fixed, more information has to be given. Write what information could be given, and add why that information fixes it to one.
z-m-25-01.s.s3.hint.0: Choose two of the equations with sum 3 and first write what differs between them so that they can be told apart.
z-m-25-01.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what information would fix that differing part to one.
z-m-25-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If we also tell the ... of the two roots, then ...
z-m-25-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check yourself that b and c are really fixed to one when you put in the information you wrote?
z-m-25-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write distinguishing which coefficient the sum connects to and which coefficient the product connects to?
z-m-25-01.s.s3.model.0: We can also tell the product of the two roots. The sum is 3, so b is fixed, and the product fixes c, so the equation is fixed to one.
z-m-25-01.s.s3.model.1: We can tell that one root is 1. The sum is 3, so the other root is fixed as 2, and if we know both roots we can write the equation, so it is fixed to one.

z-m-25-02.title: Can two examples show that an integer root must exist?
z-m-25-02.topic: Integer roots of a cubic equation: testing a generalization with counterexamples
z-m-25-02.goal: Evaluate how much examples test a claim, and show that the generalization does not hold by making a cubic equation with no integer roots yourself.
z-m-25-02.material: Minho claims, "A cubic equation x³+ax+b=0 (x cubed plus a x plus b equals 0) made with integers a and b must have an integer root." As evidence, he gave x³−x=0 (roots −1, 0, 1) and x³−4x=0 (roots −2, 0, 2).
z-m-25-02.thinking.0: Evaluating how well examples test a claim
z-m-25-02.thinking.1: Making counterexamples that fit the conditions yourself
z-m-25-02.thinking.2: Explaining the basis for being sure there is no integer root
z-m-25-02.prereq.0: This task assumes you have learned equations and inequalities in high school Common Math. "H3" is only a difficulty division of this production batch and does not mean this content is assigned to a particular grade.
z-m-25-02.prereq.1: You know factoring of polynomials and divisors and multiples of integers.
z-m-25-02.prereq.2: If there is an integer root, how that value relates to the constant term is something you observe yourself in the task.
z-m-25-02.s.s1.prompt: The two examples Minho gave are weak for testing the claim. Choose the most fitting reason.
z-m-25-02.s.s1.hint.0: Read the constant term of each of the two equations x³−x and x³−4x.
z-m-25-02.s.s1.hint.1: Check what happens when you plug in x=0 when the constant term is 0.
z-m-25-02.s.s1.o.a: Both equations have constant term b equal to 0, so x=0 is automatically a root
z-m-25-02.s.s1.r.a: If two examples share the same feature, they are not two different examples but practically one example of the same kind. You found this point.
z-m-25-02.s.s1.o.b: Both equations have negative a, so none of the roots are real
z-m-25-02.s.s1.r.b: The roots of both equations are real numbers. Write the roots of the two examples yourself and look again for the feature they share.
z-m-25-02.s.s1.o.c: Two examples is too few and weak, and three or more is always enough
z-m-25-02.s.s1.r.c: The kind of example matters more than the number of examples. Examples with the same feature have the same weakness even if there are three.
z-m-25-02.s.s1.o.d: In both equations, all the roots are integers, which makes them counterexamples to this claim
z-m-25-02.s.s1.r.d: Examples with many integer roots support the claim and are not counterexamples. Think again about what a "counterexample" breaks.
z-m-25-02.s.s1.explain: If b=0, then x(x²+a)=0, so x=0 is a root. If you collect only such examples, you can never meet the case "with no integer root".
z-m-25-02.s.s2.prompt: When a and b are integers, b is not 0, and |b| is at most 6, make 3 different (a, b) for which x³+ax+b=0 has no integer roots at all.
z-m-25-02.s.s2.hint.0: Count how many integer root candidates remain if you set b to 1 or −1.
z-m-25-02.s.s2.hint.1: Plug the candidate integers directly into the expression and find an a that keeps it from becoming 0.
z-m-25-02.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be integers.
z-m-25-02.s.s2.ok.c2: b is not 0 and |b| is at most 6.
z-m-25-02.s.s2.fail.c2: In this task, you make examples where b is not 0 and |b| is at most 6.
z-m-25-02.s.s2.ok.c3: None of x=±1, ±2, …, ±6 is a root, and 0 is not a root either, so there is no integer root.
z-m-25-02.s.s2.fail.c3: Among x=±1, …, ±6 there is a value that is a root. Plug that value into the expression and check.
z-m-25-02.s.s2.explain: For example, if x³+x+1=0 has an integer root x, then x(x²+1)=−1, so x must be 1 or −1, the divisors of 1. But plugging in gives 3 and −1, so neither is a root. There is an equation with no integer root, so Minho's claim does not hold. Still, the graph of a cubic expression always meets the x-axis, so there is a real root, and it is simply not an integer.
z-m-25-02.s.s3.prompt: Choose one of the equations you made and write why you are sure it has no integer root. Include which values you tested and why testing only those values is enough.
z-m-25-02.s.s3.hint.0: Look at the expression x(x²+a)=−b and think about which numbers an integer root, if there is one, must be a divisor of.
z-m-25-02.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many integers remain to be tested and calculate them one by one.
z-m-25-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you give the reason why integers other than the ones I tested cannot be roots?
z-m-25-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you actually check the results of the substitution calculations?
z-m-25-02.s.s3.model.0: If x³+x+1=0 has an integer root, it must be 1 or −1, the divisors of the constant term 1. Plugging in gives 3 and −1, which are not 0, so there is no integer root.
z-m-25-02.s.s3.model.1: If a=2, b=1, plugging in x=1 gives 4 and x=−1 gives −2, so neither is 0. An integer root can only be a divisor of 1, but neither is, so there is no integer root.

z-m-25-03.title: Seoyun's solution multiplying both sides: where did it go off?
z-m-25-03.topic: Inequalities with fractions: checking a solution that multiplies by an expression of unknown sign
z-m-25-03.goal: Test by plugging in values the solution that says the solution is "all real numbers except 2", find the line where the solution went off, and find the correct solution.
z-m-25-03.material:
Seoyun solved the inequality x/(x−2) > 1 (x divided by x minus 2 is greater than 1). All numbers are real numbers and x is not 2. Seoyun's solution is as follows.
1. Multiply both sides by x−2: x > x−2
2. Rearranging gives 0 > −2, which is always true.
3. Therefore all real numbers with x−2 ≠ 0 are solutions.
4. Answer: x is all real numbers except 2.
z-m-25-03.thinking.1: Finding the line where the error arose
z-m-25-03.thinking.2: Fixing and solving by splitting by sign
z-m-25-03.prereq.0: This task assumes you have learned equations and inequalities in high school Common Math. "H3" is only a difficulty division of this production batch and does not mean this content is assigned to a particular grade.
z-m-25-03.prereq.1: You can solve linear inequalities, and you know that the direction of the inequality sign flips when both sides are multiplied by a negative number.
z-m-25-03.prereq.2: You know that the value that makes the denominator of a fraction 0 is undefined.
z-m-25-03.s.s1.prompt: If Seoyun's answer is right, x/(x−2) > 1 must hold for any real number other than 2 that you plug in. Plug in directly and choose all the values for which the inequality does not hold.
z-m-25-03.s.s1.hint.0: Choose a few numbers that belong to Seoyun's answer, calculate the value of the fraction directly, and compare with 1.
z-m-25-03.s.s1.hint.1: Test a number greater than 2 and a number less than 2, and observe on which side the problem arises.
z-m-25-03.s.s1.r.a: 3/(3−2)=3, which is greater than 1, so it holds. To find a value that conflicts with Seoyun's answer, you must choose a value for which it does not hold.
z-m-25-03.s.s1.r.b: 0/(0−2)=0, which is not greater than 1. It is in Seoyun's answer but does not satisfy the original inequality.
z-m-25-03.s.s1.r.c: 5/(5−2)=5/3, which is greater than 1, so it holds. This value does not conflict with Seoyun's answer.
z-m-25-03.s.s1.r.d: 1/(1−2)=−1, which is not greater than 1. It is in Seoyun's answer but does not satisfy the original inequality.
z-m-25-03.s.s1.explain: 0 and 1 are in Seoyun's answer but do not satisfy the original inequality. So Seoyun's final answer is wrong.
z-m-25-03.s.s2.prompt: Choose the first line in Seoyun's solution where the condition stops fitting.
z-m-25-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write separately the result of multiplying both sides when x−2 is positive and when it is negative.
z-m-25-03.s.s2.hint.1: When x=0, compare the two expressions x and x−2 in line 1, and compare with the result of the original inequality.
z-m-25-03.s.s2.line.0: Multiply both sides by x−2: x > x−2
z-m-25-03.s.s2.line.1: Rearranging gives 0 > −2, which is always true.
z-m-25-03.s.s2.line.2: Therefore all real numbers with x−2 ≠ 0 are solutions.
z-m-25-03.s.s2.line.3: Answer: x is all real numbers except 2.
z-m-25-03.s.s2.explain: In line 1, both sides were multiplied by x−2 without knowing its sign. If x−2 is negative (x<2), the direction of the inequality flips and it becomes x < x−2, which is false. So the values with x<2 look like solutions even though they are not.
z-m-25-03.s.s3.prompt: Find the solution with a correct method. The method is up to you. Write how you thought about solving it and the final solution.
z-m-25-03.s.s3.hint.0: First solve only the case where x−2 is positive and write the range of x that comes out.
z-m-25-03.s.s3.hint.1: Solve the case where x−2 is negative in the same way and combine the results of the two cases.
z-m-25-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you plug one value that is in your solution and one value that is not into the original inequality to check?
z-m-25-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: How did my solution handle what was missing in Seoyun's solution (the cases by sign)?
z-m-25-03.s.s3.model.0: Multiplying only when x−2 is positive keeps the inequality sign, so x>x−2 is true. If x−2 is negative, the sign flips and it becomes x<x−2, which is false. So the solution is x>2.
z-m-25-03.s.s3.model.1: Moving the 1 on the right to the left and combining the fractions gives 2/(x−2) > 0. The numerator 2 is positive, so the denominator x−2 must also be positive, so x must be greater than 2.
z-m-25-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: Another method that solves by moving terms and combining fractions instead of multiplying

z-m-25-04.title: If k changes, does the number of solutions change too?
z-m-25-04.topic: Equations with absolute values: how the number of solutions changes
z-m-25-04.goal: Interpret the absolute value as a distance on the number line, and predict step by step, and correct, how the number of solutions changes with the value of k.
z-m-25-04.material: On a number line there are point 1 and point 3. We look for x such that |x−1|+|x−3| (the absolute value of x minus 1 plus the absolute value of x minus 3), the sum of the distance from point x to point 1 and the distance to point 3, equals k. All numbers are real numbers.
z-m-25-04.thinking.0: Predicting the number of solutions by interpreting as distances
z-m-25-04.thinking.1: Revising a prediction with new information
z-m-25-04.thinking.2: Explaining the case with infinitely many solutions
z-m-25-04.prereq.0: This task assumes you have learned equations and inequalities in high school Common Math. "H3" is only a difficulty division of this production batch and does not mean this content is assigned to a particular grade.
z-m-25-04.prereq.1: You know that |x−a| is the distance between x and a on the number line.
z-m-25-04.prereq.2: You have experience solving expressions with absolute value signs by splitting into cases.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.prompt: Predict how many solutions the equation |x−1|+|x−3|=k has each time the value of k changes.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate the sum for a few numbers x less than 1, between 1 and 3, and greater than 3.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.hint.1: Plug in x=0, 1, 2, 3, 4, make a table of the sums, and observe the change.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.0.info: First think about the case k=4.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: How many solutions are there when k=4?
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.0.after: If x=0, then 1+3=4, and if x=4, then 3+1=4, and no other x gives 4. The solutions are two, 0 and 4.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You thought there is no point at all where the sum of distances is 4. Plug in x=0 and calculate the value.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You thought that by symmetry there is only one point in the middle. Think about the outside of points 1 and 3.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a prediction that found one on each side of points 1 and 3.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You looked only at the values when x is between 1 and 3. Check whether 4 comes out in that interval.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.1.info: When x=2, the sum of distances is 1+1=2, and when x=1.5, it was also 0.5+1.5=2. This time it is k=2.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: How many solutions are there when k=2?
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.1.after: For x from 1 to 3, |x−1|=x−1 and |x−3|=3−x, so the sum is (x−1)+(3−x)=2, constant regardless of x. So there are infinitely many solutions.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You already calculated that the sum is 2 at x=2. Look at this information again.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: There are only two solutions, x=1 and x=3
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: It is true that the sum is 2 at the two points, but also check the values between them.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: There is only one solution, x=2
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This does not match the information that the sum is also 2 at x=1.5.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This matches the information that the sum is 2 at many values between 1 and 3.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Between 1 and 3 (including both ends), the sum is always 2, and outside it, the sum is greater than 2.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the range of k for which there are exactly 2 solutions?
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.2.after: If k>2, there is one solution outside the interval on the left and one on the right, so 2. If k=2, there are infinitely many, and if k<2, there are none. Your first judgment of "2" at k=4 connects to this conclusion.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The sum of distances is at least 2, so to be a value greater than 2, there is one on each side outside the interval.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: When k=2, there are not 2 solutions but infinitely many.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: k is greater than 0 and less than 4
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: There were 2 solutions at k=4, so there must be 2 also for 4 or more.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: The minimum value of the sum is 2, so if k is less than 2 there are no solutions.
z-m-25-04.s.s1.reflect: Your first judgment of 2 solutions at k=4 did not change and became one case of a broader rule. On the other hand, at k=2 the intuition of "two points" had to be corrected with new information. At which step did you keep your judgment and at which step did you correct it?
z-m-25-04.s.s2.prompt: Write what range of x the whole set of solutions is when k=2, and explain to a friend why it is not "two".
z-m-25-04.s.s2.hint.0: Plug in x=1, x=3, x=2 each and calculate the sum.
z-m-25-04.s.s2.hint.1: For x in between, write the expressions with the absolute value signs removed from |x−1| and |x−3| and add them.
z-m-25-04.s.s2.placeholder: Example: All x that ... are solutions. Because ...
z-m-25-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check by calculation whether both ends of your range (1 and 3) are included in the solutions?
z-m-25-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you pick one point inside the interval and calculate whether the sum is really 2?
z-m-25-04.s.s2.model.0: All numbers from 1 to 3 are solutions. For example, x=2 gives 1+1=2 and x=1.5 gives 0.5+1.5=2. Between 1 and 3, whatever one side increases, the other decreases by the same amount, so the sum is always 2.
z-m-25-04.s.s2.model.1: The solutions are 1≤x≤3. In this interval, |x−1|=x−1 and |x−3|=3−x, so when added, x disappears and it is always 2.

z-m-25-05.title: Checking by substitution and writing the condition first: can we trust both?
z-m-25-05.topic: Irrational equations: comparing two ways to filter out false roots created by squaring
z-m-25-05.goal: Compare two ways to filter out false roots in an irrational equation, find the case that one method misses, and judge how each method is used.
z-m-25-05.material:
Two students solved the equation √(2x+3) = x (the square root of 2x+3 equals x). All numbers are real numbers.
Gaeun: Squaring both sides gives x²−2x−3=0, that is, x=3 or x=−1. Plugging both values into the original equation, only x=3 works (√9=3).
Doyun: The value of a square root is at least 0, so first I write x≥0. Squaring gives x=3 or x=−1, and among these the one satisfying x≥0 is 3.
Both answers are x=3.
z-m-25-05.thinking.0: Comparing the validity of two methods
z-m-25-05.thinking.1: Finding the condition missing from a solution
z-m-25-05.thinking.2: Justifying your choice of method with reasons
z-m-25-05.prereq.0: This task assumes you have learned equations and inequalities in high school Common Math. "H3" is only a difficulty division of this production batch and does not mean this content is assigned to a particular grade.
z-m-25-05.prereq.1: You know that the square root √A is defined only when A is at least 0 and that its value is at least 0.
z-m-25-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose the most fitting judgment from comparing the two solutions.
z-m-25-05.s.s1.hint.0: Plug x=−1 into the left side and the right side of the original equation √(2x+3)=x and calculate each.
z-m-25-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write in one line each what basis the two used to filter out the false root, and compare.
z-m-25-05.s.s1.o.a: Only Gaeun's solution is valid. Writing the condition before solving is deciding the answer before calculating
z-m-25-05.s.s1.r.a: This judgment sees fixing the range before solving as deciding the answer in advance. Look at which numbers the condition excludes from the start.
z-m-25-05.s.s1.o.b: Only Doyun's solution is valid. Plugging in the values found is not accepted as a method
z-m-25-05.s.s1.r.b: This judgment did not accept checking by substitution as a method. Check directly with x=−1 whether substitution filters out false roots.
z-m-25-05.s.s1.o.c: Both solutions are wrong. x=−1 also works when squared, so the solutions are 3 and −1
z-m-25-05.s.s1.r.c: This judgment treats what holds in the squared equation and what holds in the original equation as the same. Plug x=−1 into the original equation.
z-m-25-05.s.s1.o.d: Both solutions are valid. They only differ in when the false root is filtered out
z-m-25-05.s.s1.r.d: This judgment sees the two methods as doing the same job at different times.
z-m-25-05.s.s1.explain: Checking by substitution is after finding, and writing the condition first narrows the range before finding. In this equation, they give the same result. In the next step, test whether the conditions of the two methods always do the same job.
z-m-25-05.s.s2.prompt: Jiho solved another equation, √(3x+1) = x−1. The way of writing the condition is similar to Doyun's. Choose the wrong line in the solution.
z-m-25-05.s.s2.hint.0: Plug x=0 and x=5 into the left side and the right side of the original equation and compare the two values.
z-m-25-05.s.s2.hint.1: Write side by side the condition Doyun used (the sign of the value of the square root) and the condition Jiho used, and see what differs.
z-m-25-05.s.s2.line.1: Rearranging gives x²−5x=0, so x=0 or x=5.
z-m-25-05.s.s2.line.2: The inside of √ must be at least 0, so write the condition 3x+1≥0, that is, x≥−1/3.
z-m-25-05.s.s2.line.3: Both 0 and 5 satisfy x≥−1/3, so the solutions are x=0 or x=5.
z-m-25-05.s.s2.explain: The condition in line 3 is only that the inside of √ is at least 0. In the equation, the value of the square root √(3x+1) must equal x−1, so x−1 must also be at least 0. If x=0, then √1=1 but x−1=−1, so they are not equal. So x=0 in line 4 is not a solution, and the solution is x=5 only.

z-m-25-06.title: The same equation but 2 answers and 4 answers? Find the missing information
z-m-25-06.topic: Quartic equations: the number of solutions depending on the range of numbers in which solutions are sought
z-m-25-06.goal: Know that the reason different numbers of solutions come out for the same equation is the range of numbers in which solutions are sought, make equations that fit the conditions, and say what information is needed.
z-m-25-06.material: Mina and Hyunwoo found the number of solutions of the equation x⁴+x²−6=0 (x to the fourth plus x squared minus 6 equals 0), but their answers were different. Both let x²=t and solved identically up to (t+3)(t−2)=0. Mina said, "There are 2 solutions," and Hyunwoo said, "There are 4 solutions."
z-m-25-06.thinking.0: Finding the missing information in conflicting answers
z-m-25-06.thinking.1: Designing expressions that fit the conditions yourself
z-m-25-06.thinking.2: Revising the question so that the answer is fixed to one
z-m-25-06.prereq.0: This task assumes you have learned equations and inequalities in high school Common Math. "H3" is only a difficulty division of this production batch and does not mean this content is assigned to a particular grade.
z-m-25-06.prereq.1: You know the imaginary unit i (the square of i is −1) and complex numbers.
z-m-25-06.prereq.2: You know the method of substituting to turn the equation into a quadratic form and solving it (in this task, you do not have to use that method).
z-m-25-06.s.s1.prompt: For both answers to be correct answers, what information should we say is missing from the problem?

z-m-25-06.s.s1.hint.1: Write which collection of x each of Mina's 2 and Hyunwoo's 4 is.

z-m-25-06.s.s1.r.a: With this condition the only solution is x=√2, so neither answer is correct.
z-m-25-06.s.s1.o.b: There is an additional condition that t must be an integer
z-m-25-06.s.s1.r.b: t is 2 and −3, which are already integers. This condition does not separate the two answers.

z-m-25-06.s.s1.o.d: There is an additional condition that all coefficients are integers
z-m-25-06.s.s1.r.d: The coefficients are already all integers. This condition does not separate the two answers.
z-m-25-06.s.s1.explain: If t=2, x=±√2 (real), and if t=−3, x=±i√3 (imaginary). In the real number range there are 2, and in the complex number range there are 4.

z-m-25-07.title: Two integer roots whose product is greater than their sum: which roots work?

z-m-25-07.goal: Design quadratic equations that satisfy conditions on the product and sum of the two roots, and explain the pairs of roots to avoid as a rule.
z-m-25-07.material: You design a quadratic equation x²−px+q=0 (p and q are integers). There are three conditions. (1) The two roots are different positive integers. (2) The product q of the two roots is greater than the sum p of the two roots. (3) p and q are integers. All numbers are considered in the real numbers.
z-m-25-07.thinking.1: Designing examples that satisfy the conditions at the same time
z-m-25-07.thinking.2: Generalizing and explaining the cases to avoid
z-m-25-07.prereq.0: This task assumes you have learned equations and inequalities in high school Common Math. "H3" is only a difficulty division of this production batch and does not mean this content is assigned to a particular grade.

z-m-25-07.prereq.2: You know the discriminant and perfect squares of integers.
z-m-25-07.s.s1.prompt: If one of the two roots is 1, what can you say about the sizes of the product and the sum? (Let the other root be an integer n that is at least 2.)
z-m-25-07.s.s1.hint.0: Make a table of the product and the sum when one root is 1 and the other is 2, 3, 4.
z-m-25-07.s.s1.hint.1: Look at how the difference between the product and the sum comes out in the table.

z-m-25-07.s.s1.r.d: This judgment relies on a feeling that the product is bigger. For 1 and 3, the product is 3 and the sum is 4. Compare directly.
z-m-25-07.s.s1.explain: If the roots are 1 and n, the product is n and the sum is n+1, so the product is always 1 less than the sum. So an equation with one root equal to 1 cannot satisfy (2).
z-m-25-07.s.s2.prompt: Choose p and q and make 3 different x²−px+q=0 that satisfy all the conditions (1), (2), (3).

z-m-25-07.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the product is greater than the sum, and if not, change the roots and try again.

z-m-25-08.title: For how many seconds is the height 15 m or more?
z-m-25-08.topic: Applying quadratic inequalities: judging the solution interval under changing conditions
z-m-25-08.goal: Predict how the solution interval of a quadratic inequality changes when the information in the situation changes, and reflect the range limit of the situation in the solution.
z-m-25-08.material: A ball is thrown upward from the ground, and its height after t seconds is h(t) = −5t² + 20t (meters). We consider the ball only from the moment of the throw (t=0) until it touches the ground again (t=4). We look at intervals such as the time when the height is 15 m or more and the time when it is 10 m or less. √1.2 is about 1.095 and √2 is about 1.414.
z-m-25-08.thinking.0: Predicting the direction and length of an interval
z-m-25-08.thinking.1: Revising the solution interval when conditions change
z-m-25-08.thinking.2: Reflecting the limits of the situation in the solution
z-m-25-08.prereq.0: This task assumes you have learned equations and inequalities in high school Common Math. "H3" is only a difficulty division of this production batch and does not mean this content is assigned to a particular grade.
z-m-25-08.prereq.1: You can solve quadratic inequalities by connecting them with the graph of a quadratic function.

z-m-25-08.s.s1.prompt: Predict the range of t each time the situation changes.

z-m-25-09.title: Can P(1) and P(3) alone fix the remainder?
z-m-25-09.topic: The remainder theorem: information that fixes the remainder to one
z-m-25-09.goal: Tell apart the information that can be used to fix the remainder from the information that cannot, and refute an error by making different remainders that satisfy the same information.
z-m-25-09.material: The remainder R(x) when the polynomial P(x) is divided by (x−1)(x−2) is an expression of the form ax+b of degree at most 1. The expression of P(x) is not known, and only some function values of P(x) may be given. (a and b are real numbers)
z-m-25-09.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-25-09.thinking.1: Finding an unjustified substitution in a solution
z-m-25-09.prereq.0: This task assumes you have learned equations and inequalities in high school Common Math. "H3" is only a difficulty division of this production batch and does not mean this content is assigned to a particular grade.
z-m-25-09.prereq.1: You know the polynomial division expression P(x)=B(x)Q(x)+R(x) and the degree of the remainder.
z-m-25-09.prereq.2: You know the remainder theorem (the remainder when P(x) is divided by x−a is P(a)).
z-m-25-09.s.s1.prompt: Which of the following is information that fixes the remainder R(x) to one?
z-m-25-09.s.s1.hint.0: In P(x)=(x−1)(x−2)Q(x)+ax+b, plug in the known values of x and observe what happens to the term with the quotient Q(x).
z-m-25-09.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many equations in a and b you can set up from the information in each option.
z-m-25-09.s.s1.r.a: Think about whether a and b are fixed to one when there is only one piece of information. There are many (a, b) with a+b=3.
z-m-25-09.s.s1.r.b: This judgment uses the information at the two values that make the divisor (x−1)(x−2) equal to 0.
z-m-25-09.s.s1.r.c: This may be a judgment that applied the information at x=3, which is not a value that makes the divisor 0, directly to the remainder. Check whether the quotient part of the division expression becomes 0 at x=3.
z-m-25-09.s.s1.r.d: This is information that lacks all the values that make the divisor 0. Think about whether you can set up equations in a and b with this information.
z-m-25-09.s.s1.explain: In P(x)=(x−1)(x−2)Q(x)+ax+b, plugging in x=1 and x=2 removes the effect of the quotient, so P(1)=a+b and P(2)=2a+b. If you know these two values, a and b are fixed (a=2, b=1).
z-m-25-09.s.s2.prompt: A student found the remainder using only 'P(1)=3, P(3)=7'. Choose the wrong line in the solution.
z-m-25-09.s.s2.hint.0: Write out the expression P(3)=2Q(3)+3a+b obtained by plugging in x=3 and compare it with line 3.
z-m-25-09.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate the value of (x−1)(x−2) when x=1 is plugged into the expression in line 1 and when x=3 is plugged in.
z-m-25-09.s.s2.line.0: If the quotient when P(x) is divided by (x−1)(x−2) is Q(x) and the remainder is ax+b, then P(x)=(x−1)(x−2)Q(x)+ax+b.
z-m-25-09.s.s2.line.1: Plugging in x=1 gives P(1)=a+b, so a+b=3.
z-m-25-09.s.s2.line.2: Plugging in x=3 gives P(3)=3a+b, so 3a+b=7.
z-m-25-09.s.s2.line.3: Solving the two equations gives a=2, b=1, so the remainder is 2x+1.
z-m-25-09.s.s2.explain: In line 3, when x=3 is plugged in, (x−1)(x−2)Q(3)=2Q(3) is not 0, but the term with the quotient was dropped. So 3a+b=7 may not hold. The conclusion in line 4 also relies on this.
z-m-25-09.s.s3.prompt: There are polynomials with P(1)=3 and P(3)=7 whose remainder is not 2x+1. When the remainder is ax+b, make 3 different (a, b) for which such a polynomial can exist. (Exclude the case a=2.)
z-m-25-09.s.s3.hint.0: First write what relationship between a and b arises when you write P(1)=3 in terms of the remainder.
z-m-25-09.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether P(3)=7 can be satisfied if you take the quotient Q to be a constant.
z-m-25-09.s.s3.var.a: The coefficient a of x in the remainder
z-m-25-09.s.s3.var.b: The constant term b of the remainder
z-m-25-09.s.s3.ok.c1: P(1)=3 also holds for the remainder (a+b=3).
z-m-25-09.s.s3.fail.c1: Check again what a+b must be for P(1)=3.
z-m-25-09.s.s3.fail.c2: If a=2, then b=1 and it is 2x+1. Find other values.
z-m-25-09.s.s3.explain: Taking P(x)=(x−1)(x−2)Q+ax+b (Q is a constant), P(1)=a+b=3 and P(3)=2Q+3a+b=7. If a+b=3, you can match with Q=2−a, so even if a is not 2, there are polynomials that satisfy both conditions. Example: if a=1, b=2, Q=1, then P(x)=x²−2x+4 and P(1)=3, P(3)=7, but the remainder is x+2.

z-m-25-10.thinking.1: Designing coefficients that fit the conditions
z-m-25-10.thinking.2: Explaining the conclusion by splitting into cases

z-m-25-10.prereq.1: You can solve simultaneous linear equations with two unknowns.
z-m-25-10.prereq.2: You know that one solution, no solution, and infinitely many solutions are all possible.
z-m-25-10.s.s1.prompt: When you know only the value of a and not the value of b, what can you say about the number of solutions?

z-m-25-11.title: Hayun's solution by replacing with |x|: where did the negative numbers go?
z-m-25-11.topic: Quadratic inequalities with absolute values: finding the gap in a solution
z-m-25-11.goal: Using substitution, check the solution that disappeared in the last line of a solution that substituted |x|, and write the correct solution set as intervals.
z-m-25-11.material: Hayun solved the inequality x²−4|x|+3<0 (x squared minus 4 times the absolute value of x plus 3 is less than 0) and answered, "The solution is 1<x<3." All numbers are real numbers.
z-m-25-11.thinking.1: Finding the wrong line in a solution
z-m-25-11.prereq.0: This task assumes you have learned equations and inequalities in high school Common Math. "H3" is only a difficulty division of this production batch and does not mean this content is assigned to a particular grade.
z-m-25-11.prereq.1: You know the meaning of the absolute value sign |x| and x²=|x|².
z-m-25-11.prereq.2: You can write the solutions of quadratic inequalities and absolute value inequalities |x|>a, |x|<a as intervals.
z-m-25-11.s.s1.prompt: If Hayun's answer is right, numbers that are not 1<x<3 must not satisfy the inequality. Plug in directly and choose all the values for which the inequality holds.
z-m-25-11.s.s1.hint.0: Choose a few numbers inside and outside Hayun's interval and calculate the value of the expression.
z-m-25-11.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate, paying attention to what the value of |x| is when you plug in a negative number.
z-m-25-11.s.s1.r.a: If you plug in 0, the value is 3, which is not less than 0. It does not hold.
z-m-25-11.s.s1.r.b: 4−8+3=−1, so it holds. It is a value inside Hayun's interval.
z-m-25-11.s.s1.r.c: 9−12+3=0, which is not less than 0. A boundary value is excluded for the inequality sign <.
z-m-25-11.s.s1.r.d: 4−8+3=−1, so it holds. It is a value outside Hayun's interval, so it conflicts with Hayun's answer.
z-m-25-11.s.s1.explain: x=2 is inside Hayun's interval, and x=−2 holds even though it is outside the interval. So Hayun's answer left out some of the solutions.
z-m-25-11.s.s2.prompt: This is Hayun's solution. Choose the wrong line.
z-m-25-11.s.s2.hint.0: Choose directly, from −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, the x that satisfy |x|>1.
z-m-25-11.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the conclusion in line 4 includes x=−2.
z-m-25-11.s.s2.explain: In line 4, the solution of |x|>1 was written only as x>1. |x|>1 is x>1 or x<−1. So the solution on the x<−1 side disappeared.
z-m-25-11.s.s3.prompt: Fix Hayun's solution, write the correct solution as intervals, and write in a line or two how you found it.
z-m-25-11.s.s3.hint.0: Write how |x| can be written when x≥0 and when x<0.
z-m-25-11.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether the interval from each case overlaps with the condition of that case.
z-m-25-11.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does my solution include both x=−2 and x=2?
z-m-25-11.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check that the boundary values −3, −1, 1, 3 are not included in the solution?
z-m-25-11.s.s3.model.0: |x|>1 is x>1 or x<−1. So the solution of 1<|x|<3 is −3<x<−1 or 1<x<3, and x=−2 is included too.
z-m-25-11.s.s3.model.1: When x≥0, it is x²−4x+3<0, so 1<x<3. When x<0, it is x²+4x+3<0, so −3<x<−1. Combining the two cases gives −3<x<−1 or 1<x<3.

z-m-25-12.title: How many cubic equations have all three roots as integers?
z-m-25-12.topic: Integer roots of cubic equations: finding all possible coefficients
z-m-25-12.goal: Under the condition that all three roots are integers, find several possible triples of roots, and explain why the possible equations are finitely many.
z-m-25-12.material: For integers a and b, there is a cubic equation x³+ax²+bx−6=0 (x cubed plus a x squared plus b x minus 6 equals 0). We look for the cases where all three roots of this equation are integers. Repeated roots are also allowed.
z-m-25-12.thinking.1: Finding several solutions within the conditions
z-m-25-12.thinking.2: Explaining why the number of cases is finite
z-m-25-12.prereq.0: This task assumes you have learned equations and inequalities in high school Common Math. "H3" is only a difficulty division of this production batch and does not mean this content is assigned to a particular grade.
z-m-25-12.prereq.1: You know the relationship between the three roots and the coefficients of a cubic equation (the relationship between roots and coefficients).
z-m-25-12.prereq.2: You know the divisors of integers.
z-m-25-12.s.s1.prompt: When all three roots are integers, choose the number that cannot be one of the roots.
z-m-25-12.s.s1.hint.0: Plug an integer root r into the equation, gather the constant term 6 on one side, and see whether you can factor out r.
z-m-25-12.s.s1.hint.1: Find the product of the three roots and check how it relates to 6.
z-m-25-12.s.s1.r.a: If −6 is a root, then −216+36a−6b−6=0, so it is possible with b=6a−37. Divisors of the constant term 6 can be roots.
z-m-25-12.s.s1.r.b: 2 is a divisor of 6 and can be a root. For example, there is the case where the roots are 1, 2, 3.
z-m-25-12.s.s1.r.c: This is a choice made by thinking about what relationship the value must have with the constant term when a root is an integer.
z-m-25-12.s.s1.r.d: −1 is a divisor of 6 and can be a root. There is the case where the roots are −1, −2, 3.
z-m-25-12.s.s1.explain: If there is an integer root r, then r³+ar²+br=6, that is, r(r²+ar+b)=6, so r must be a divisor of 6. 4 is not a divisor of 6, so it cannot be a root.
z-m-25-12.s.s2.prompt: Writing the three roots in order from smallest as r1≤r2≤r3, find 4 different (r1, r2, r3) for which all three roots are integers and are roots of x³+ax²+bx−6=0.
z-m-25-12.s.s2.hint.0: Find all sets of three integers whose product is 6, splitting into the case where all are positive and the case where two negative numbers are mixed in.
z-m-25-12.s.s2.hint.1: For each combination you find, calculate the product of the three roots and check that it is 6.
z-m-25-12.s.s2.fail.c1: All three roots must be integers.
z-m-25-12.s.s2.ok.c2: They are written in order from smallest.
z-m-25-12.s.s2.fail.c2: They must be written in order from smallest to largest (equal values are allowed).
z-m-25-12.s.s2.ok.c3: The product of the three roots is 6, which matches the constant term −6.
z-m-25-12.s.s2.fail.c3: The constant term of the expression made from the three roots is not −6.
z-m-25-12.s.s2.explain: If the three roots are r1, r2, r3, the constant term is −r1r2r3, so the product is 6. The cases where the product of three integers is 6 are (1,2,3), (1,1,6), (−1,−1,6), (−1,−2,3), (−1,−3,2), (−2,−3,1), (−6,−1,1), seven in all. For example, if (1,2,3), then a=−6, b=11.
z-m-25-12.s.s3.prompt: Are there infinitely many or finitely many (a, b) that satisfy this condition? Write your judgment and the reason.
z-m-25-12.s.s3.hint.0: From the condition that the product of the three roots is 6, think about how large a single root can be.
z-m-25-12.s.s3.hint.1: Write down all the cases you found and count them.
z-m-25-12.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the number of cases I wrote match the number I actually counted?
z-m-25-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you state that swapping the order of the three roots counts as the same case?
z-m-25-12.s.s3.model.0: Finite. The product of the three roots is fixed at 6, and the combinations of three integers whose product is 6 are limited, so (a, b) also comes out only that many times.
z-m-25-12.s.s3.model.1: Finite. The product of three integers is 6, so the absolute value of each root is at most 6, and the possible cases can all be listed, so there are only about 7.

z-m-25-13.title: If both the sum and the product are positive, are both roots positive?
z-m-25-13.topic: Relationship between roots and coefficients: a counterexample to "the sum and product are positive"
z-m-25-13.goal: Find and make a counterexample to the claim "if the sum and the product are both positive, both roots are positive", and fix the condition so that the claim becomes true.
z-m-25-13.material: Jisu says about the quadratic equation x²−px+q=0 (p and q are real numbers), "If the sum p and the product q are both positive, both roots are positive." As evidence, she gives x²−5x+6=0 (roots 2, 3) and x²−7x+10=0 (roots 2, 5). Here we consider roots in the complex numbers.
z-m-25-13.thinking.2: Fixing the condition under which a claim holds
z-m-25-13.prereq.0: This task assumes you have learned equations and inequalities in high school Common Math. "H3" is only a difficulty division of this production batch and does not mean this content is assigned to a particular grade.
z-m-25-13.prereq.1: You know the relationship between roots and coefficients (the sum and product of the two roots).
z-m-25-13.prereq.2: You know the discriminant and imaginary roots (roots that are not real numbers).
z-m-25-13.s.s1.prompt: Choose the equation that can be a counterexample that breaks Jisu's statement. (A counterexample must satisfy Jisu's assumption but not satisfy the conclusion.)
z-m-25-13.s.s1.hint.0: Read p and q of each equation and keep only those that satisfy Jisu's assumption (p>0, q>0).
z-m-25-13.s.s1.hint.1: Check the sign of the discriminant of the remaining equations to see whether the roots are real.
z-m-25-13.s.s1.r.a: With p=4, q=4, it satisfies the assumption, but the root is a single 2 (a double root), which is positive, so the conclusion also holds. It is not a counterexample.
z-m-25-13.s.s1.r.b: p=−3, so it does not satisfy the assumption (p>0). To be a counterexample, it must satisfy the assumption.
z-m-25-13.s.s1.r.c: q=−4 is negative, so it does not satisfy the assumption (q>0).
z-m-25-13.s.s1.r.d: With sum p=2 and product q=5 it satisfies the assumption, but the roots are 1±2i, so the conclusion does not hold.
z-m-25-13.s.s1.explain: The sum 2 and the product 5 are both positive, but the roots are the non-real 1±2i. It satisfies the assumption and fails the conclusion, so it is a counterexample.
z-m-25-13.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different (p, q) for x²−px+q=0 with p>0, q>0 but whose two roots are not both positive. (p and q are real numbers)
z-m-25-13.s.s2.hint.0: After choosing p and q to be positive, check the sign of p²−4q.
z-m-25-13.s.s2.hint.1: Change p to be small and q to be large so that the sign becomes negative.
z-m-25-13.s.s2.ok.c1: The sum and the product are both positive.
z-m-25-13.s.s2.fail.c1: The sum p and the product q must both be positive.
z-m-25-13.s.s2.ok.c2: The two roots are not real, so they are not "both positive".
z-m-25-13.s.s2.fail.c2: With this (p, q), it is not a case where the two roots are not both positive. Check the discriminant.
z-m-25-13.s.s2.explain: If p>0, q>0 and the discriminant p²−4q<0, the roots are imaginary, so "both roots are positive" does not hold. (2,5) has the imaginary roots 1±2i, and (1,1) has the imaginary roots (−1±i√3)/2. Conversely, (5,6) has the two roots 2, 3, both positive, so it is not a counterexample.
z-m-25-13.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite Jisu's statement so that it becomes true. Write what condition must be added and why both roots become positive when that condition holds.
z-m-25-13.s.s3.hint.0: Write what property was different in the counterexample (2, 5) that broke the claim.
z-m-25-13.s.s3.hint.1: Add in one line a condition that prevents that property.
z-m-25-13.s.s3.selfAssess.0: If you apply the condition you added to Jisu's counterexample (2, 5), does the counterexample disappear?
z-m-25-13.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does the explanation include what the signs of the two roots are when the sum is positive and the product is positive?
z-m-25-13.s.s3.model.0: In addition to p>0, q>0, we need the condition that the roots are real, that is, the discriminant p²−4q≥0. The product is positive, so the two roots have the same sign, and the sum is positive, so both are positive.
z-m-25-13.s.s3.model.1: We need to add the condition that the two roots are real. If the roots are real and the product is positive, they have the same sign, and the sum is positive, so both are positive.
